claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its as-cast simple solid-solution state.
A simple single-phase solid solution provides minimal obstacles to dislocation motion in CoCrFeNiTi.
CoCrFeNiTi has near-uniform atomic sizes and limited lattice distortion.
Near-uniform atomic environments and limited lattice distortion produce very low lattice friction.
Significant short-range order, precipitates, and other dislocation barriers are scarce in the starting state.
Low lattice friction and scarce barriers promote facile dislocation glide and dynamic recovery.
The applicable starting material is nominally equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in an as-cast, homogeneous, single-phase FCC or BCC state with minimal secondary phases.
Room-temperature, quasi-static tensile and compression testing combined with pre- and post-deformation TEM and EBSD can probe the proposed dislocation behavior.
The relevant structural mediator is dislocation density and mobility in a homogeneous lattice lacking precipitates, nanotwins, and pronounced short-range order.
Weak solid-solution hardening permits easy dislocation nucleation and motion.
Rapid dynamic recovery limits work hardening and thereby caps hardness and strength.
The unaged alloy should have lower yield strength and work-hardening rate than comparable high-entropy alloys containing additional strengthening features.
TEM and EBSD should show predominantly free dislocation glide with sparse pile-ups or barrier formation.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates by aging provides a controlled strengthened comparison to the untreated as-cast state.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate at ambient temperature under quasi-static deformation.
Severe plastic deformation, aging, or extreme test temperatures may change the governing behavior.
Subtle short-range ordering or minor composition fluctuations may contribute to dislocation pinning.
Observation of dominant hidden strengthening features or strong dislocation impediments in the as-cast material would falsify the proposed facile-glide mechanism.
